content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn: This work focuses on detecting microaggressions by exploring multiple models and comparing how these models generalize (e.g., from real-world examples to TV shows). Reviewers agreed that it aims at a very interesting and important topic of using context to better detect microaggression, with diverse datasets and clear presentation. Major concerns are the lack of comparison with existing models in this domain (as discussed in their related work) and comprehensive evaluation, as well as the lack of descriptive details regarding experimental setup. No author response was submitted. I recommend not accepting the current version and encouraging the authors to improve their work based on the reviewers' suggestions.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper describes evaluation of Micro aggression classifier using variations of n-grams, ML algorithms and data sets. 

The paper uses off the shelf ML algorithms, variations of BERT and SVM. While the data sets considered are new, not much comprehensive evaluation and publication of the data sets is provided for cross check. Some of the claims look suspicious. 

1. how can number of words and number of comments be so close (page 4), unless, the words per comment Is  mostly 1
2. why don’t we have full P/R curve or AuROC to gauge performance curve - just looking at the P/R/F numbers is not helpful.
3. imbalance class problem - it is not addressed at all, except 90% and 10% selection. A baseline should have been provided.

Overall, while the paper aims to make in roads in an area that is important and often overlooked. It is unclear how this expedition can be used by the practitioners, owing to specificity of the data set and above issues.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of detecting microaggressions. The paper aims to investigate several models on the task, especially focusing on the extent of leveraging context. Also, it aims to look into how well the models trained on real-world examples work for microaggressions on TV shows.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The topic is interesting (studying the effect of context in detecting microaggression)
- easy to follow overall

Weaknesses:
- the contributions of this paper were not clear to me in light of the previous work, by reading the paper (especially Sec 2)
- I can see that the paper focuses on the differences of the models, trying to interpret the results to draw some conclusions. However, in my opinion, the differences among the different models are too simplified, and then are used for interpretation of the experiment results. Therefore, I was not really convinced by some of the claims/interpretations. I will list them in the detailed comments. 
- It is not only real life vs. media. <= are there any other differences in the format, style of the data, etc.? for example, the real life data are from social media and survey/interviews, and the media data are TV show scripts, which are totally different. How do you think this might have affected the experiment results?
- Further analysis on detected microagression would be interesting. 

Detailed comments are below. Major and minor comments are mixed.
- why vectorizing documents using tf-idf in the data collection process?
- 70% cosine similarity score as a threshold? What did you compare? how did you compute cosine similarity scores? between those tf-idf vectors?
- punctuation removal <= removing punctuation is OK. I'm just wondering if punctuations could help with MA detection, because they sometimes express more nuanced things such as strength of emotions, etc. 
- what is "text decontraction"?
- ultimately => Ultimately
- "there do not appear to be distinguishing patterns of N-grams, as these models perform equally to the unigram models."
"Because the performance is similar, the terms that are indicative of MAs are likely specific to the text. "
<= How can we know these? Did you look at the output of different models to see if those models agree on each document?
- context <= how is context defined in this work? I think all the methods use contextual clues to some extent in different ways. 
- The abstract talks about different senses of "context" (e.g., workplace, social media), which makes "context" a bit more confusing
- HateBERT has the same architecture as BERT but is optimized for overt hate speech <= how was it optimized?
- I think the differences among different models are too simplified, and then are used for interpretation of the experiment results. 
- It is not only real life vs. media. <= are there any differences in the format, style of the documents, etc.? for example, the real life documents are essays and the other documents are scripts, which are totally different. 
- Some analysis on microagression would have been interesting. 
- "dependent on incorporating contextual clues" <= would be helpful if you can elaborate on this
- examples of the statements that were not convincible to me:
--- "there do not appear to be distinguishing patterns of N-grams, as these models perform equally to the unigram models."
"Because the performance is similar, the terms that are indicative of MAs are likely specific to the text. "
<= How can we know these only looking at those numbers? Did you look at the output of different models to see if those models agree on each document? 
--- "One alternative explanation is ...."
--- "suggesting that MAs occur in similar, but not identical ways across domains"

content.summary_of_the_paper: The work used 7,764 dataset scrapped from the web and collected from survey sources to identify Microaggressions in real-life and scripted conversations. It applied the SVM classifier using bag-of-word vectorizations, and the transformer model RoBERTa, putting into use N-gram and bag-of-word approaches to further understand the nature of Microaggressions and the extent to which varying amounts of contexts impacts on it. The result shows that Microaggressions  in real-life are very complex and contextually dependent where its expression in art are similar to its expression in life. However, a disconnect between the contexts of microaggressions found in Art and those from real-life was observed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths 
1. The article was well written and theory based. 
2. The approaches discussed are in line with the state of the art in the domain 
3. The dataset used was reasonably sufficient
4. The choice of the evaluation metrics are OK. 

Weaknesses: 
1. The discussion of the Results did not sufficiently compare the work to existing works in the domain. The discussion section is poor. 
2. The experimental setup was not shown; the tools used was not presented. No form of schematic diagram to demonstrate the flow of operations. 
3. Since a real-life  and TV setting was involved, the model deployment would have been presented to show readiness for real-life usage. This was not done or shown. 
4. Few grammar errors were observed. 
5. The work did not show any benchmark model (results) to access improvements either in the literature review or discussion section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The work done is moderately clear (though not in details to convey reproducibility). The quality of the article is scientifically sound and the exploration of the Microaggressions in hate speech research demonstrated in the work is novel and original.
content.summary_of_the_review: The work shows that all the models explored performed better with a real life data than with a scripted one thereby validating the contextual nature of Microaggression. Also. there was no significant difference in results in the different variations with the SVM Model as well as the Transformer Model. Despite the good strengths of the work, it is my view that the weaknesses seems big but can be improved upon to bring the work to an acceptable stage.

content.title: Towards Identification of Microaggressions in real-life and Scripted conversations, using Context-Aware Machine Learning Techniques.
content.TL;DR: Classification of microaggressions from text data (extracted from real life conversation, social media platforms and classic TV shows) using SVMs and RoBERTA, considering the impact of varying amounts of context on overall models' performance.
content.abstract:
The advent and rapid proliferation of social media have brought with it an exponential growth in hate speech and overt offensive language, with one of the most subtle yet pervasive subcategories of hate speech being Microaggressions (MA). MAs are unintentional, hostile, derogatory, or negative prejudicial slights and insults toward any group, particularly culturally marginalized communities and growing bodies of research are linking long-term MA exposure to serious health problems. The scarcity of studies leveraging AI techniques to identify MAs in text and in spoken conversations, coupled with the lack of investigative analysis on the impact of context on the performance of algorithms used for this task, makes this a relevant topic for the AI community. In this paper, we explore the degree of effectiveness of MAs detection often found in spoken human communications across various contexts (e.g., workplace, social media, conversations) using Machine Learning models. We further examine the extent that art may imitate life, by comparing the ability of these models trained on real-life conversations to infer MAs, occurring in scripted Television shows. We apply a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier using N-grams and contextual modeling representation, using the Robustly Optimized Bidirectional Encoder Representation for Transformer (RoBERTa) model, whose performance is evaluated based on its pretraining size and ability to accurately detect hate speeches, with comparative results from BERT based-uncased and the HateBERT model respectively. 
Overall, the results show that contextual transformer models outperform simpler context-free approaches to classifying MAs collected from surveys and online blogs. We also found that these models trained on real-life conversations could infer MAs in scripted TV settings, though at reduced levels, and equal rates, suggesting there may be a disconnect between contexts of MA found in art and those from real life.
